current.alt: Labelled light microscope showing eyepiece, objective lenses, stage, focusing knobs and light source
current.caption: Figure: The light microscope. Light passes up through the specimen on the stage; the objective and eyepiece lenses magnify it, and the coarse then fine focusing knobs sharpen the image.

current.alt: Rod-shaped bacterial cell in cross section with labels in left and right columns for cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, circular DNA, plasmid and flagella
current.caption: Figure: A bacterial (prokaryotic) cell. There is no nucleus and no mitochondria: the DNA is a single circular chromosome free in the cytoplasm, with extra genes on small plasmids.

current.alt: Labelled sequence for preparing a temporary microscope slide with specimen, stain, cover slip and filter paper
current.caption: Figure: Preparing a temporary slide. The specimen must be thin enough for light to pass through; the cover slip is lowered at an angle so no air bubbles are trapped.

current.alt: Four specialised cells in a row — red blood cell, sperm cell, root hair cell and palisade cell — each named by a label directly beneath it
current.caption: Figure: Specialised cells. Each shape serves its function — the biconcave disc gives a large surface area for oxygen, the tail moves the sperm, the hair extension increases water uptake and the packed chloroplasts absorb light.

current.alt: Rod-shaped bacterial cell in cross section with labels in left and right columns for cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, circular DNA, plasmid and flagella
current.caption: Figure: Bacterial structure revisited. Compare this with the animal and plant cells on page 3: the missing nucleus and membrane-bound organelles are the defining prokaryotic features.

current.alt: Four specialised cells in a row — red blood cell, sperm cell, root hair cell and palisade cell — each named by a label directly beneath it
current.caption: Figure: Specialisation in detail. Read each cell as structure → function: identify the adapted feature first, then state the job it makes possible.

current.alt: Labelled sequence from cell to tissue, organ, whole organism and population in a habitat
current.caption: Figure: Levels of organisation. Similar cells form a tissue, tissues form an organ, organs work together in the organism, and organisms of one species form a population.

current.alt: Labelled diagram of diffusion across a cell membrane showing high and low concentration and net movement
current.caption: Figure: Diffusion. Particles move randomly in all directions, but because more start on the crowded side there is a net movement down the concentration gradient until it is equalised.

current.alt: Labelled diagram of osmosis showing water crossing a partially permeable membrane while large solute molecules cannot
current.caption: Figure: Osmosis. Water molecules are small enough to cross the partially permeable membrane; the larger solute molecules are not, so water moves towards the more concentrated solution.

current.alt: Labelled diagram of active transport showing a carrier protein moving particles against the concentration gradient using energy from a mitochondrion
current.caption: Figure: Active transport. A carrier protein pumps particles from a low to a high concentration, so unlike diffusion it needs energy released by respiration in mitochondria.

current.alt: Labelled agar-cube diffusion practical showing cubes of different sizes in purple potassium manganate(VII) solution and a cut cube with a stained rim
current.caption: Figure: Investigating diffusion. The same depth of dye enters every cube, so the small cube — with the largest surface area to volume ratio — becomes fully stained first.

current.alt: Three plotted graphs showing rate of photosynthesis against light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature
current.caption: Figure: Limiting factors. Rate rises with light or carbon dioxide until it plateaus because another factor is now limiting; with temperature the rate falls again above the optimum because the enzymes denature.

current.alt: Leaf cross section with labels in left and right columns for waxy cuticle, upper epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll, air spaces, xylem, phloem, lower epidermis and stoma with guard cells
current.caption: Figure: Cross-section through a leaf. Palisade cells near the upper surface are packed with chloroplasts; air spaces in the spongy layer let carbon dioxide diffuse to them from the stomata below.

current.alt: Labelled diagram comparing an open stoma with swollen guard cells and a closed stoma with limp guard cells
current.caption: Figure: Stomata control gas exchange. When guard cells take in water they swell and bow apart, opening the pore; when they lose water they go limp and the pore closes, which limits water loss but also limits carbon dioxide entry.

current.alt: Labelled apparatus for measuring photosynthesis rate using pondweed, a lamp and a ruler
current.caption: Figure: Measuring the rate of photosynthesis. Oxygen bubbles from the pondweed are collected in the test tube; moving the lamp changes light intensity, which is the variable under test.

current.alt: Leaf cross section with labels in left and right columns for waxy cuticle, upper epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll, air spaces, xylem, phloem, lower epidermis and stoma with guard cells
current.caption: Figure: Leaf structure. Every feature serves photosynthesis — the transparent epidermis lets light through to the chloroplast-packed palisade layer, the air spaces let carbon dioxide reach the cells, and the xylem delivers water.

current.alt: Three tomato plants compared: full mineral supply, no nitrate showing stunted pale growth, and no magnesium showing yellowing between the veins
current.caption: Figure: Mineral ions and growth. Nitrate is needed to make amino acids and proteins for growth, while magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll — so each deficiency produces its own recognisable symptom.

current.alt: Three plotted graphs showing rate of photosynthesis against light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature
current.caption: Figure: Limiting factors. Rate rises with light or carbon dioxide until it plateaus because another factor is now limiting; with temperature the rate falls again above the optimum because the enzymes denature.

current.alt: Leaf cross section with labels in left and right columns for waxy cuticle, upper epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll, air spaces, xylem, phloem, lower epidermis and stoma with guard cells
current.caption: Figure: Leaf structure. Every feature serves photosynthesis — the transparent epidermis lets light through to the chloroplast-packed palisade layer, the air spaces let carbon dioxide reach the cells, and the xylem delivers water.

current.alt: Three tomato plants compared: full mineral supply, no nitrate showing stunted pale growth, and no magnesium showing yellowing between the veins
current.caption: Figure: Mineral ions and growth. Nitrate is needed to make amino acids and proteins for growth, while magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll — so each deficiency produces its own recognisable symptom.

current.alt: Labelled four-stage practical for testing a leaf for starch using boiling water, ethanol, rinsing and iodine solution
current.caption: Figure: Testing a leaf for starch. Boiling kills the leaf and makes it permeable, ethanol removes the green chlorophyll so the colour change is visible, and iodine turns blue-black only where starch is present.

current.alt: Balanced diet plate labelled with nutrient functions
current.caption: Teaching point: A balanced diet supplies suitable proportions of nutrients, fibre and water rather than equal amounts of every food.

current.alt: Four test tubes showing positive food-test colours for starch, reducing sugar, protein and fat
current.caption: Figure: Positive food-test results. Iodine turns blue-black with starch, heated Benedict’s solution gives a brick-red precipitate with reducing sugar, biuret turns lilac with protein and the ethanol test gives a cloudy white emulsion with fat.

current.alt: Labelled grassland food chain showing grass, grasshopper, small bird and kestrel joined by arrows
current.caption: Figure: A food chain. The arrows point in the direction that energy and biomass are transferred, starting with the producer that captured the light energy by photosynthesis.

current.alt: Labelled apparatus for measuring the energy content of a food sample by burning it under a boiling tube of water
current.caption: Figure: Food energy. The energy released by the burning food warms a measured mass of water, so the temperature rise lets the energy per gram of food be calculated.

current.alt: Labelled grassland food chain showing grass, grasshopper, small bird and kestrel joined by arrows
current.caption: Figure: A food chain. The arrows point in the direction that energy and biomass are transferred, starting with the producer that captured the light energy by photosynthesis.

current.alt: Labelled apparatus for measuring the energy content of a food sample by burning it under a boiling tube of water
current.caption: Figure: Food energy. The energy released by the burning food warms a measured mass of water, so the temperature rise lets the energy per gram of food be calculated.

current.alt: Diagram of a container divided by a partially permeable membrane, with a dilute solution on the left and a concentrated solution on the right, small water molecules on both sides, large solute molecules mostly on the right, and an arrow showing net water movement to the right
current.caption: Figure: Osmosis. Water molecules cross the membrane in both directions, but because there is a higher proportion of water on the dilute side more move to the right, giving a net movement down the water concentration gradient. The solute molecules are too large to pass through.

current.alt: Osmosis in plant cells and the root-to-leaf water pathway
current.caption: Teaching point: Water movement changes plant-cell turgor and supplies the transpiration stream through xylem.

current.alt: Diagram of a container divided by a partially permeable membrane, with a dilute solution on the left and a concentrated solution on the right, small water molecules on both sides, large solute molecules mostly on the right, and an arrow showing net water movement to the right
current.caption: Figure: Osmosis. Water molecules cross the membrane in both directions, but because there is a higher proportion of water on the dilute side more move to the right, giving a net movement down the water concentration gradient. The solute molecules are too large to pass through.

current.alt: Labelled diagram of a root hair cell among soil particles, showing the long narrow hair, nucleus, vacuole, cell wall and membrane, with arrows for water entering the hair
current.caption: Figure: The root hair cell. Its long, narrow shape gives a very large surface area in contact with soil water, so water can enter rapidly by osmosis while mineral ions are taken in by active transport against their concentration gradient.

current.alt: Three plant cells compared: a turgid cell with the membrane pressed against the wall, a flaccid cell with the contents slightly shrunken, and a plasmolysed cell whose membrane has pulled away from the wall
current.caption: Figure: Turgid, flaccid and plasmolysed cells. The rigid cell wall stops the cell bursting, so a cell in pure water becomes turgid; as the surrounding solution becomes more concentrated water leaves, the cell becomes flaccid, and finally the membrane pulls away from the wall — plasmolysis.

current.alt: Labelled diagram of a root hair cell among soil particles, showing the long narrow hair, nucleus, vacuole, cell wall and membrane, with arrows for water entering the hair
current.caption: Figure: The root hair cell. Its long, narrow shape gives a very large surface area in contact with soil water, so water can enter rapidly by osmosis while mineral ions are taken in by active transport against their concentration gradient.

current.alt: Diagram of a plant stem in section showing a xylem channel with upward arrows and a phloem channel with downward arrows, leaves losing water vapour and roots absorbing water
current.caption: Figure: Xylem and phloem. Xylem carries water and mineral ions upwards only, pulled by evaporation from the leaves; phloem carries dissolved sugars away from the leaves either up or down, which is translocation.

current.alt: Plotted graph with a rising curve that levels off for light, temperature and air movement, and a falling curve for humidity, with a key explaining both
current.caption: Figure: Rate of transpiration. Anything that speeds evaporation from the leaf raises the rate until the stomata are fully open, whereas humid air reduces the concentration gradient out of the leaf and slows transpiration.

current.alt: Plotted graph with a rising curve that levels off for light, temperature and air movement, and a falling curve for humidity, with a key explaining both
current.caption: Figure: Rate of transpiration. Anything that speeds evaporation from the leaf raises the rate until the stomata are fully open, whereas humid air reduces the concentration gradient out of the leaf and slows transpiration.

current.alt: Four beakers of increasing sucrose concentration, each holding a potato cylinder, with the cylinders shown progressively smaller and the mass change stated beneath each
current.caption: Figure: The prescribed practical. Cylinders in dilute solutions gain mass because water enters by osmosis, and cylinders in concentrated solutions lose mass because water leaves; the concentration at which there is no change matches the cell contents.

current.alt: Four beakers of increasing sucrose concentration, each holding a potato cylinder, with the cylinders shown progressively smaller and the mass change stated beneath each
current.caption: Figure: The prescribed practical. Cylinders in dilute solutions gain mass because water enters by osmosis, and cylinders in concentrated solutions lose mass because water leaves; the concentration at which there is no change matches the cell contents.

current.alt: Diagram of a plant stem in section showing a xylem channel with upward arrows and a phloem channel with downward arrows, leaves losing water vapour and roots absorbing water
current.caption: Figure: Xylem and phloem. Xylem carries water and mineral ions upwards only, pulled by evaporation from the leaves; phloem carries dissolved sugars away from the leaves either up or down, which is translocation.

current.alt: Labelled human digestive system showing mouth, oesophagus, stomach, liver, pancreas, small intestine, large intestine and rectum
current.caption: Figure: The human digestive system. Food travels from the mouth down the oesophagus to the stomach, then through the small intestine where digestion finishes and absorption happens, and finally through the large intestine to the rectum.

current.alt: Lock-and-key model showing substrate binding to an enzyme active site and products being released
current.caption: Figure: The lock-and-key model. Only a substrate with the matching shape fits the active site; the enzyme is unchanged afterwards and can be used again.

current.alt: Two plotted graphs: rate of reaction against temperature peaking at 37 degrees Celsius, and rate against pH for a stomach protease peaking at pH 2 and an intestinal amylase peaking at pH 8
current.caption: Figure: Enzymes and conditions. Warming speeds the reaction because collisions become more frequent and energetic, but above the optimum the active site changes shape permanently, and each enzyme works fastest at the pH of the region it is secreted into.

current.alt: Two beakers compared: oil floating as one large droplet, and the same oil emulsified by bile into many tiny droplets
current.caption: Figure: Emulsification. Bile is not an enzyme — it physically breaks large fat droplets into many small ones, which greatly increases the surface area on which lipase can act, so digestion is faster.

current.alt: Labelled villus showing microvilli, one-cell-thick epithelium, capillary network and lacteal
current.caption: Figure: A villus. Its thin wall, huge surface area and rich blood supply make absorption of digested food fast and efficient.

current.alt: Two plotted graphs: rate of reaction against temperature peaking at 37 degrees Celsius, and rate against pH for a stomach protease peaking at pH 2 and an intestinal amylase peaking at pH 8
current.caption: Figure: Enzymes and conditions. Warming speeds the reaction because collisions become more frequent and energetic, but above the optimum the active site changes shape permanently, and each enzyme works fastest at the pH of the region it is secreted into.

current.alt: Diagram of an enzyme and its complementary substrate fitting into the active site
current.caption: Figure: Enzyme specificity. Only a substrate whose shape is complementary to the active site can bind, which is why each digestive enzyme acts on one type of food molecule.

current.alt: Two beakers compared: oil floating as one large droplet, and the same oil emulsified by bile into many tiny droplets
current.caption: Figure: Emulsification. Bile is not an enzyme — it physically breaks large fat droplets into many small ones, which greatly increases the surface area on which lipase can act, so digestion is faster.

current.alt: Labelled diagram of a villus showing epithelium, blood capillaries and lacteal
current.caption: Figure: Absorption. Villi provide a very large, thin, well-supplied surface, so absorption by diffusion and active transport is rapid.

current.alt: Two plotted graphs: rate of reaction against temperature peaking at 37 degrees Celsius, and rate against pH for a stomach protease peaking at pH 2 and an intestinal amylase peaking at pH 8

current.alt: Labelled diagram of the human alimentary canal
current.caption: Figure: The alimentary canal. Each region carries out a specific stage, so food is broken down in the right order before absorption.

current.alt: Four labelled panels showing plasma, a red blood cell, a white blood cell and a platelet, each with a note on its structure and function
current.caption: Figure: The components of blood. Plasma is the liquid transport medium, red blood cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin, white blood cells defend against microbes, and platelets help the blood to clot.

current.alt: Four labelled panels showing plasma, a red blood cell, a white blood cell and a platelet, each with a note on its structure and function
current.caption: Figure: The components of blood. Plasma is the liquid transport medium, red blood cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin, white blood cells defend against microbes, and platelets help the blood to clot.

current.alt: Cross sections of an artery with a thick wall and narrow lumen, a vein with a thin wall and wide lumen, and a capillary with a wall one cell thick
current.caption: Figure: Blood vessels in cross section. The artery wall is thick and muscular to withstand high pressure, the vein has a wide lumen and valves for low-pressure return flow, and the capillary wall is one cell thick so diffusion distances are short.

current.alt: Four labelled panels showing plasma, a red blood cell, a white blood cell and a platelet, each with a note on its structure and function

current.alt: Labelled pathway of blood through the heart, lungs and body
current.caption: Teaching point: Double circulation sends deoxygenated blood to the lungs and oxygenated blood to body tissues in separate circuits.

current.alt: Labelled front view of the heart showing right and left atria and ventricles, the septum, atrioventricular valves, vena cava, pulmonary artery, pulmonary vein and aorta
current.caption: Figure: Heart structure. Valves and the septum make the flow one-way and keep oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate; the left ventricle wall is thickest because it pumps blood to the whole body.

current.alt: Flow diagram of lungs, heart and body organs with arrows showing the pulmonary circuit and the systemic circuit
current.caption: Figure: Double circulation. Blood returns to the heart between the two circuits, so it is re-pressurised before travelling to the body organs — this delivers oxygen far faster than a single circulation could.

current.alt: Flow diagram of lungs, heart and body organs with arrows showing the pulmonary circuit and the systemic circuit
current.caption: Figure: Double circulation. Blood returns to the heart between the two circuits, so it is re-pressurised before travelling to the body organs — this delivers oxygen far faster than a single circulation could.

current.alt: Line graph of pulse rate in beats per minute against time in minutes, rising from a resting value during exercise and falling gradually during recovery
current.caption: Figure: Pulse rate and exercise. The rate rises during exercise because muscles need more oxygen and glucose and must remove more carbon dioxide; the speed of the fall afterwards is a measure of fitness.

current.alt: Line graph of pulse rate in beats per minute against time in minutes, rising from a resting value during exercise and falling gradually during recovery
current.caption: Figure: Pulse rate and exercise. The rate rises during exercise because muscles need more oxygen and glucose and must remove more carbon dioxide; the speed of the fall afterwards is a measure of fitness.

current.alt: Diagram of a capillary above a block of respiring muscle tissue, with arrows showing oxygen and glucose diffusing out of the blood and carbon dioxide diffusing in
current.caption: Figure: Exchange at a capillary. The one-cell-thick wall, slow blood flow and very large surface area of a capillary bed all shorten diffusion distances and speed up exchange with respiring tissue.

current.alt: Labelled front view of the heart showing right and left atria and ventricles, the septum, atrioventricular valves, vena cava, pulmonary artery, pulmonary vein and aorta

current.alt: Labelled mitochondrion showing outer membrane, inner membrane, cristae and matrix
current.caption: Figure: A mitochondrion, the site of aerobic respiration. The folded inner membrane (cristae) gives a large surface area for the reactions that release energy from glucose.

current.alt: Labelled breathing system and enlarged alveolus
current.caption: Teaching point: Alveoli provide a large, thin, moist exchange surface beside capillaries for oxygen and carbon dioxide diffusion.

current.alt: Labelled human breathing system showing nasal cavity, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli, lungs, ribs and diaphragm
current.caption: Figure: The human breathing system. Air passes through the trachea and bronchi into ever-smaller bronchioles that end in millions of alveoli.

current.alt: Labelled diagram of the human breathing system
current.caption: Figure: The breathing system. Ventilation moves air to and from the alveoli, where the gas exchange that supplies respiration actually happens.

current.alt: Labelled alveolus with a one-cell-thick wall surrounded by capillaries containing red blood cells
current.caption: Figure: An alveolus. Oxygen diffuses across the thin, moist wall into the blood while carbon dioxide diffuses out; the surrounding capillaries keep the concentration gradient steep.

current.alt: Plotted graph of breathing rate in breaths per minute against time, showing a resting rate, a rise during exercise and a gradual fall during recovery
current.caption: Figure: Exercise and recovery. Breathing rate rises to deliver oxygen and remove carbon dioxide faster; it stays raised after exercise stops so the extra oxygen can break down the lactic acid that built up — the oxygen debt.

current.alt: Plotted graph of breathing rate in breaths per minute against time, showing a resting rate, a rise during exercise and a gradual fall during recovery

current.alt: Labelled apparatus for investigating fermentation: yeast and glucose in a sealed flask in a water bath, with a delivery tube leading to limewater
current.caption: Figure: Testing for fermentation. The bung excludes oxygen so the yeast respires anaerobically, and the carbon dioxide produced turns the limewater milky, confirming the reaction.

current.alt: Labelled diagram of an alveolus and its surrounding capillary showing oxygen and carbon dioxide diffusion
current.caption: Figure: Gas exchange. A thin, moist, well-ventilated and well-supplied surface keeps steep diffusion gradients for both gases.

current.alt: Labelled male and female reproductive systems
current.caption: Teaching point: The labelled structures produce and transport gametes and support fertilisation and development.

current.lesson: 2.4 Genome, Chromosomes, Genes, DNA and Genetics
current.alt: Cell-to-gene hierarchy and a labelled monohybrid Punnett square
current.caption: Teaching point: Genes are sections of DNA carried on chromosomes; the Punnett square predicts possible offspring genotypes.

current.alt: Four-stage diagram of natural selection causing antibiotic resistance
current.caption: Teaching point: Antibiotics select from existing variation: resistant bacteria survive and reproduce rather than changing because they need resistance.
